title: Brevetoxin exposure, blood analytes, and reproductive success in nesting loggerhead sea turtles and their offspring, SW Florida.
authors: Kelly A Sloan, Nicole I Stacy, Justin R Perrault, et al.
summary: After a massive Florida red-tide bloom, scientists measured the algal toxin 'brevetoxin' in nesting loggerhead turtles and their eggs. Mothers passed the toxin on to their eggs and hatchlings, and nests carrying more toxin had fewer hatchlings emerge successfully.
key_points: Toxin from the 2017-2019 red tide showed up in nesting loggerheads, their unhatched eggs, and dead hatchlings
Turtles feeding in the Gulf of Mexico carried more toxin than those foraging in the Atlantic
Higher toxin in hatchling livers was linked to lower nest emergence success
why_it_matters: Red-tide blooms may quietly harm sea turtle health and reproduction, piling another stressor onto already endangered populations.

title: Presuming pathways of sea turtles using stable isotopes from shells of epibiont barnacles.
authors: Kyungsik Jo, Jeongmin Kim, Byung-Yeob Kim, Taewon Kim
summary: Instead of electronic tags, researchers read the chemistry of barnacle shells growing on stranded sea turtles to reconstruct where those turtles had travelled. The barnacles' oxygen and carbon 'signatures' traced routes through the Taiwan Strait, the Philippines, and the Ryukyu Islands toward Korea.
key_points: Chemical signatures locked in barnacle shells act as a natural travel log of their turtle host
The method reconstructed migration paths for loggerhead and hawksbill turtles found near Jeju Island, Korea
It can reveal journeys where electronic satellite tags are impractical or unavailable
why_it_matters: A cheap, tag-free way to reconstruct sea turtle migrations helps target conservation in hard-to-monitor ocean regions.

title: Simulating 135 years of post-hatchling sea turtle dispersal in a dynamic North Atlantic Ocean.
authors: Michael D Arendt, Nathan F Putman
summary: Using an ocean-circulation model, researchers simulated how loggerhead hatchlings from the U.S. East Coast drifted across the Atlantic over 135 years. Most drifted toward the Azores, and the amount of eastward drift rose over the last century alongside warming seas and stronger currents.
key_points: Six million virtual hatchlings were tracked through 135 years of simulated Atlantic currents
68% drifted east past 60 degrees W, most ending up near the Azores
Drift was lowest around 1896-1900 and highest a century later, tracking climate shifts
why_it_matters: Linking ocean climate to where hatchlings drift helps predict how warming seas will reshape sea turtle populations.

title: Tracking rehabilitated sea turtles in the Indian Ocean using satellite telemetry: behaviour, ecology, and conservation.
authors: Katrina Himpson, Thomas Le Berre, Edward Hodges
summary: Researchers satellite-tagged olive ridley, green, and hawksbill turtles after rehabilitating and releasing them in the Indian Ocean. The rehabilitated turtles survived well and behaved like wild ones, with monsoon-driven currents strongly steering their journeys.
key_points: Released rehab turtles survived for long periods and behaved like wild individuals
Monsoon-driven ocean currents strongly shaped their open-ocean movements
Adds rare tracking data for under-studied olive ridley and juvenile turtles
why_it_matters: Evidence that rehabilitation works supports rescue programs and shows why cross-border cooperation matters for wide-ranging turtles.

title: Comparative analysis of the mucosal and shell microbiota of the invasive red-eared slider across urban freshwater habitats.
authors: Mariangel Correa Orellana, Justin C Havird, et al.
summary: Researchers swabbed 42 invasive red-eared slider turtles across urban ponds in Austin, Texas, mapping the bacteria on their shells and skin and inside their mouths and guts. Where on the body a sample came from mattered most for which microbes were present, though the pond location mattered too.
key_points: 142 samples revealed over 20,000 distinct bacterial types across five body locations
Body location shaped the microbial community most strongly; habitat had a smaller effect
First-ever description of the mouth (oral) microbiome in red-eared sliders
why_it_matters: Invasive turtles in city waters can carry and spread microbes, so surveying them helps monitor urban ecosystems and public health.

title: Molecular cloning and pathogen-induced expression of interleukin-18 in the Chinese soft-shelled turtle.
authors: Zhihui Xiao, Jiehao Xu, Chutian Ge, Xiaodong Zhang, et al.
summary: Scientists in China identified and cloned an immune-signalling gene (interleukin-18) in the farmed Chinese soft-shelled turtle. When turtles were exposed to bacteria or a virus, this gene ramped up, showing it is an active part of the turtle's immune defence.
key_points: The full IL-18 immune gene was cloned and characterized in the Chinese soft-shelled turtle
Bacterial and viral challenges boosted the gene's activity in the spleen and liver
A lab-made version of the protein triggered other immune responses, confirming it works
why_it_matters: Understanding turtle immune genes can help fight the diseases that plague soft-shelled turtle aquaculture, an important food industry.

title: Comparative transcriptomic analysis of the thymus and immune tissues from stranded cetaceans in South Korea.
authors: Ju-Sung Kim, Kyunglee Lee, HyeongJin Roh, et al.
summary: Researchers examined immune-system tissues from stranded whales and dolphins in Korea and compared their gene activity with many other animals, including green and loggerhead sea turtles. Even in post-mortem samples each tissue kept a distinct genetic fingerprint, with the thymus showing the richest set of immune genes.
key_points: Immune tissues were compared across mammals, fish, birds, and reptiles including sea turtles
The thymus carried the widest variety of active immune genes
Aquatic animals leaned on 'alternative' immune pathways rather than classic antigen-presentation routes
why_it_matters: Mapping how aquatic animals defend themselves builds a baseline for diagnosing disease in whales, dolphins, and sea turtles.

title: Highly Contiguous Is Not Chromosomally Accurate: Integrated Cytogenetic and Genomic Mapping in Two Turtle Genome.
authors: Anastasia A Proskuryakova, Katerina V Tishakova, Maria M Kulak, Arina V Ilina, Sergey A Marchenko, Lada S Lisachova, Guzel I Davletshina, Elena I Shagimardanova, Alessio Iannucci, Vladimir A Trifonov, Svetlana A Romanenko
summary: Scientists created detailed genetic maps of two turtle species by combining traditional chromosome imaging techniques with modern DNA sequencing data. They discovered that even when genome assemblies look complete and well-organized, they can contain mistakes in how chromosomes are actually arranged, highlighting the need to double-check genetic maps with physical evidence.
key_points: High-quality genome assemblies can still have errors in chromosome structure that aren't caught by sequencing alone
Using chromosome-specific probes and physical mapping techniques can reveal mistakes that computational methods miss
One turtle species' assembly was accurate while the other had a false rearrangement, showing these problems are unpredictable
These errors could lead to incorrect conclusions about how species evolved and how genes are organized
why_it_matters: Accurate genome maps are critical for medical research, understanding evolution, and finding genes, so validating them with multiple methods prevents costly mistakes in downstream research.

title: Fatal coinfection by Mycobacterium fortuitum and Epicoccum sp. with concurrent severe coccidial enteritis in an olive ridley sea turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea).
authors: Daphne Wrobel Goldberg, Daniela Farias da Nóbrega, Ana Paula Frederico R L Bracarense, et al.
summary: A stranded olive ridley turtle in Brazil died from three infections at once: a bacterium normally found in soil and water, an unusual environmental fungus, and a severe gut parasite. Vets think the parasite infection and long-term poor condition weakened the turtle enough for the other two to take hold.
key_points: The turtle arrived emaciated and lethargic and died six days later despite antibiotics and supportive care
An autopsy found inflammatory lumps across its internal organs, plus pneumonia and liver, bladder and gut inflammation
The bacterium Mycobacterium fortuitum is increasingly turning up as a disease-causing agent in marine wildlife
This is the first time the fungus Epicoccum has been recorded causing disease in a sea turtle
why_it_matters: Documenting which opportunistic infections kill debilitated turtles helps rehabilitation centres recognise and treat them earlier.

title: First Record of Triplet Embryos in Sea Turtles: Evidence of Natural Polyembryony in a Wild Green Turtle (Chelonia mydas) Nest From Guanahacabibes, Cuba.
authors: Julia Azanza-Ricardo, Annelisse Bárcenas-Ibarra, Kevin Armando Domínguez-León, et al.
summary: Researchers in Cuba found three embryos sharing a single yolk inside one green turtle egg, the first confirmed triplets from a wild sea turtle nest. All three were genetically identical, meaning one fertilised egg had split three ways.
key_points: Only one other case of triplets has ever been confirmed in any turtle or tortoise, and that was in captivity
Each embryo had its own blood supply but all three drew on one shared yolk
One embryo was badly underdeveloped with facial malformations, likely because one yolk cannot feed three
The nest was otherwise healthy, with 91.6 percent of eggs hatching successfully
why_it_matters: Rare developmental events like this only get spotted when nests are monitored over many years, which is an argument for sustained long-term fieldwork.

title: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in loggerhead sea turtles (Caretta caretta) embryos: Occurrence, tissue distribution and associated biological responses.
authors: Erica Trotta, Francesco Alessandro Palermo, Paolo Cocci, et al.
summary: Scientists tested loggerhead turtle embryos from a polluted stretch of Italian coast and found petroleum-related chemicals had passed from mothers into their eggs. The embryos' livers switched on detoxification machinery in response, showing they were actively processing the contaminants.
key_points: The pollutants, called PAHs, showed up in the yolk at every stage of development and in 70 percent of embryo livers
The more pollutant in the liver, the more strongly a detoxification gene was switched on
Despite that chemical response, no visible tissue damage was found in the embryos
Contamination varied noticeably between eggs within the same clutch
why_it_matters: Mothers passing pollution to their offspring is an exposure route that risk assessments for protected marine species often overlook.

title: A novel assessment tool to measure thermal variability on sea turtle nesting beaches.
authors: Jacques-Olivier Laloë, Holly J Stokes, Nicole Esteban, et al.
summary: How hot the sand is on a nesting beach decides whether eggs become male or female, so it needs measuring. This team showed a single logger on a one-metre steel probe can map a beach's temperature range in ten days, instead of burying many loggers for whole seasons.
key_points: Tested on four islands in the Chagos Archipelago, an important green and hawksbill turtle nesting site
Accuracy matched the continuously recording loggers normally used for this work
Season was by far the biggest influence, with a 2.9C gap between warmer and cooler months
Position along the beach mattered more, up to 1.7C, than whether the spot was shaded or exposed, 0.6C
why_it_matters: A cheap, fast way to measure nest temperatures makes it practical to monitor many more beaches as the climate warms.

title: Genomic characterization of novel human-associated CTX-M-15-producing Serratia nevei ST625 lineage infecting a vulnerable loggerhead sea turtle.
authors: Guilherme E Paiva, Fábio P Sellera, João Pedro Rueda Furlan, et al.
summary: A loggerhead turtle in a Brazilian rehabilitation centre was infected by a drug-resistant bacterium almost identical to strains previously found in human hospital patients in the same region. The two differed by only 27 genetic letters.
key_points: The bacterium resisted several major antibiotic classes, including advanced cephalosporins
Its closest known relative was a strain from a human urine sample collected in Sao Paulo in 2019
Every publicly catalogued member of this bacterial lineage had previously come from human patients
The resistance gene sat on a mobile genetic element, the kind that spreads easily between bacteria
why_it_matters: Resistant bacteria moving between people and wildlife is exactly the crossover that One Health surveillance exists to catch.

title: Chelonid alphaherpesvirus 5 qPCR of archived blood and skin samples underpredicts infections in juvenile green turtles Chelonia mydas.
authors: Jake R Kelley, Tamara Lee, Katherine R Martin, et al.
summary: Fibropapillomatosis is a tumour disease of sea turtles linked to a herpesvirus. This study tested decades of archived green turtle samples and found the standard DNA test almost never detects the virus in stored blood or skin, even when the turtle was infected.
key_points: Only 1.4 percent of 513 archived blood samples and 6.5 percent of 123 skin samples tested positive
By contrast, 89.7 percent of actual tumour samples tested positive
Samples spanned 1995 to 2018, ranging from 1 to 24 years old when tested
A negative result on old blood or skin says more about the sample than about the turtle
why_it_matters: Researchers reusing archived samples need to know a negative test is not evidence the animal was healthy, or they will badly underestimate how widespread the virus is.

title: Spirorchiidiasis in Stranded Olive Ridley Turtles (Lepidochelys olivacea) Along the Northern and Central-Northern Chilean Coast.
authors: Carlos A Flores Olivares, Juan Pablo Ruíz Yañez, Gerardo Cerda Gaete, et al.
summary: Six stranded olive ridley turtles on the Chilean coast were carrying blood flukes, parasitic worms that lodge in blood vessels and organs. The infections had caused inflammatory damage through the gut, reproductive tract and blood vessels.
key_points: All six were adult females that stranded between September 2024 and January 2026
Parasites were found in intestine, reproductive tract, blood vessels, liver, spleen and adrenal glands
Damage included thickened tissue and inflammatory lesions passing right through the gut wall
This confirms the parasite group is present in olive ridleys in Chilean waters
why_it_matters: Identifying a parasite that may be driving strandings gives managers a cause to investigate rather than an unexplained die-off.

title: Haplotypes across the Oceans: worldwide phylogeography, evolution, conservation and nomenclature standardization in the leatherback sea turtle (Dermochelys coriacea).
authors: Wesley D Colombo, Sarah de S A Teodoro, João Luiz G da Fonseca, et al.
summary: Leatherback turtle genetics has a naming problem: different studies read different lengths of DNA and gave the same genetic variants different labels. This team reviewed 304 sequences worldwide and proposed a single standard naming system.
key_points: Redundant naming had led researchers to misread how leatherback populations are structured
They settled on two standard sequence lengths, identifying 32 and 24 variants respectively
The family tree points to a Pacific origin, with later spread into the Atlantic and Indian Oceans
The modern leatherback lineage dates back roughly 4.9 million years
why_it_matters: Shared naming conventions let separate studies be combined, which is how scattered genetic data becomes usable for conservation decisions.

title: Assessment of Exposure to Essential and Non-Essential Elements through Concentrations in Tissues of Chelonia mydas (Green turtles) from the South Atlantic, Northeast Brazil.
authors: Midiã S Rodrigues, Iago J S da Silva, Cristina F da Fonseca, et al.
summary: Researchers measured eleven metals in the shells, muscle, livers and kidneys of 43 green turtles from northeastern Brazil. Cadmium, a toxic heavy metal, was far above Brazilian food safety limits in every internal tissue tested.
key_points: Kidney cadmium averaged 49 mg/kg against a legal limit of 1.0, roughly fifty times over
Likely sources include coastal fertiliser runoff and contaminated food eaten over many years
Aluminium was highest in shell and iron highest in liver
Turtles with the tumour disease fibropapillomatosis had significantly different shell copper levels
why_it_matters: Turtle tissues can double as a cheap monitoring tool for tracking pollution across a whole coastal ecosystem.

title: Traplines: A Promising Modification to Reduce Sea Turtle Bycatch in Swordfish Longlines.
authors: Paolo Casale, Vittoria Fiandino, Daniela Freggi
summary: Longline fishing hooks accidentally catch large numbers of sea turtles. This trial tested a hookless alternative called a trapline alongside conventional hooks on the same lines: the traplines caught almost no turtles while still landing plenty of fish.
key_points: Across 23 fishing sets, hooks caught 127 loggerhead turtles while traplines caught 1
Hooks landed 9711 kg of commercial fish, traplines 6580 kg from far fewer deployments
Both gear types were deployed alternately on the same line, so conditions were identical
Turtles caught per kilogram of fish was significantly better for traplines
why_it_matters: A modification that nearly eliminates turtle bycatch without gutting the catch is rare, and that combination is what makes fishers likely to adopt it.

title: Umbilical Cord: A Non-Invasive DNA Source for Sea Turtle Genomics.
authors: Gisela Marín-Capuz, Elena Abella, Marta Pascual, et al.
summary: Getting DNA from sea turtle hatchlings usually means taking blood, which is risky in such small animals. This study shows the umbilical cord left behind after hatching works just as well, and collecting it disturbs nothing.
key_points: Umbilical cord DNA matched the hatchling's own blood genotype 97.7 percent of the time
It reflects the hatchling rather than the mother, which had been an open question
Cords were present in 100 percent of artificially incubated Spanish nests but only 4.5 percent of natural nests in Cape Verde
The method therefore suits incubator-hatched eggs best
why_it_matters: A sampling method that harms nothing makes genetic monitoring far easier to justify for threatened species.

title: Effects of controlled artificial incubation on hatching success, morphometric traits, and early physiological indicators in olive ridley sea turtles (Lepidochelys olivacea) from Banyuwangi coast, Indonesia.
authors: Ragil Angga Prastiya, Suherni Susilowati, Imam Mustofa, et al.
summary: Hatcheries in Indonesia move olive ridley eggs into controlled incubators to protect them from predators and flooding. This study found the approach gives good hatching rates, but hatchlings still differ depending on which beach the eggs came from.
key_points: Overall hatching success was 83.7 percent, ranging from 77.6 to 91.4 percent by beach of origin
Incubators held a steady 28.6C and 80 percent humidity throughout
Hatchlings from different beaches differed significantly in shell length and flipper length
Faster yolk absorption went together with larger hatchlings
why_it_matters: If the source beach still shapes hatchling quality, hatcheries should track nest origin rather than treating all eggs as interchangeable.

title: Occurrence and toxicological assessment of PCDD/Fs and PCBs in loggerhead turtle eggs undergoing climate-induced nesting expansion in the southern Tyrrhenian Sea.
authors: Mauro Esposito, Sara Lambiase, Roberto Miniero, et al.
summary: Loggerhead turtles are starting to nest further north in the Mediterranean as the sea warms. Researchers tested eggs from these newly colonised Italian beaches and found persistent industrial pollutants in every one.
key_points: Dioxins and PCBs were present across the whole study area, including the newest northern nesting sites
Concentrations were high enough to pose a possible toxic risk to embryos and hatchlings
Pollution levels showed no clear link to clutch size or hatching success
Extreme weather did track with lower hatching success, and differed between north and south
why_it_matters: A species shifting range because of climate change can move straight into polluted water, so the two pressures need assessing together.

title: Surveillance of gastrointestinal viruses of free-ranging and rehabilitated Sea turtles in the United States.
authors: Weerapong Laovechprasit, Vicente A Avila-Reyes, Brian A Stacy, et al.
summary: Almost nothing was known about the viruses living in sea turtle guts. This survey sequenced 77 gut samples from six species along both US coasts and turned up 48 viruses, several never described before.
key_points: Nineteen viruses across eight families were characterised in detail
Seven appear to be entirely new species and one a new genus
Many were genetically close to viruses of fish and marine invertebrates, hinting they arrive through diet
Samples came from both healthy free-ranging turtles and sick rehabilitation cases
why_it_matters: You cannot tell which viruses threaten turtle health until you know which ones are normally present, and this is that baseline.

title: A deep learning-based fusion framework for robust fine-grained classification of sea turtles in support of marine biodiversity.
authors: Parkpoom Chaisiriprasert, Apicha Deearom
summary: Telling sea turtle species apart in underwater photos is hard because of murky water, poor light and partly hidden animals. This team built an image classifier that reads both colour and edge outlines, and it identified species more accurately than colour alone.
key_points: Built on a standard image-recognition network with an extra input channel carrying edge detail
Two different ways of combining colour and shape information were tested
The better one reached 87.2 percent average precision, beating both alternatives
Adding shape information helped most with species that look similar
why_it_matters: Automated identification lets conservation teams process survey footage at a scale no human reviewer could manage.

title: Global Characterization of Sea Turtle Ecological Traps under Compound Marine Heatwaves and Microplastics.
authors: Hao Liu, Yiling Zhong, Zehou Li, et al.
summary: Sea turtles face two growing threats at once: marine heatwaves and microplastic pollution. Combining global tracking data for seven species with ocean records, this study found turtles linger in heavily polluted zones instead of moving away from heat stress.
key_points: Turtles spent significantly longer in waters with moderate to high microplastic concentrations
Polluted areas appear to act as a false safe harbour
Inside those zones the turtles' normal instinct to swim away from hot water broke down
The result is longer exposure to heat and pollution together
why_it_matters: Conservation maps drawn as fixed protected areas miss threats like this, which move and interact, and so need dynamic management instead.

title: Stress Assessment in Caretta caretta During the Rehabilitation Period.
authors: Chiara Lomonaco, Giorgia Schiró, Paola Galluzzo, et al.
summary: Rescued loggerhead turtles in Italian rehabilitation centres were blood-tested three times over two months to see how stressed captivity made them. Stress markers were highest on arrival and fell steadily as the turtles settled in.
key_points: Twenty-five turtles were tracked, 12 juveniles and 13 near-adults
The team measured stress hormone, blood sugar, white blood cell ratios and muscle enzymes
Juveniles arrived more stressed than older turtles but showed the clearest improvement over time
Both age groups ended the two months with significantly lower stress readings than they started
why_it_matters: Knowing that handling stress fades within weeks reassures rehabilitators that the process itself is not harming the animals they are trying to save.

title: Whole-Genome Sequencing and Comparative Genomic Analysis of Citrobacter farmeri and Enterobacter cloacae from Unhatched Green Turtle Eggs.
authors: Nurcan Önen, Bahadır Törün, Can Yılmaz
summary: Bacteria from green turtle eggs that failed to hatch on a Mediterranean beach were fully genome-sequenced for the first time. Two common opportunistic species turned out to carry extensive antibiotic resistance and genes that help them invade tissue.
key_points: Samples came from infected eggshells and dead embryos across 30 nests at Akyatan Beach, Turkey
Both species resisted multiple antibiotic classes including penicillin-type drugs and fluoroquinolones
They also carried genes for sticking to tissue and scavenging iron, both useful for causing infection
Their genomes closely matched reference strains taken from human clinical infections
why_it_matters: Hatching failure is usually blamed on temperature or flooding, so identifying resistant bacteria in failed eggs opens a different line of investigation.

title: Foraging ecology of the critically endangered hawksbill sea turtle in the Gulf of Guinea.
authors: Sara Vieira, Betânia Ferreira-Airaud, Vânia Baptista, et al.
summary: Hawksbill turtles are critically endangered, and this study worked out what they eat around Sao Tome Island in the Gulf of Guinea. Chemical signatures in their skin showed sponges dominate the diet at every age, but adults branch out more than juveniles.
key_points: Thirty turtles were sampled using minimally invasive methods during in-water surveys
Adults added red algae and tunicates to the sponge diet; juveniles stuck to sponges
Juveniles stayed put in smaller areas, suggesting they settle in one place for long stretches
Both age groups feed at the level of secondary consumers in the food web
why_it_matters: You cannot protect a feeding ground without knowing what the animals eat there and which life stages depend on it.

title: Aquatic Turning Performance in Juvenile Loggerhead and Green Sea Turtles.
authors: M T Wileyto, F E Fish, S E Trail, et al.
summary: Sea turtles are famous for long-distance swimming, but nobody had measured how well they turn. Filming juvenile loggerheads and green turtles from above revealed they use two distinct turning styles and favour one flipper over the other.
key_points: Turtles chased food in a large tank while cameras tracked points on their head and shell
They performed both spinning-in-place turns and sweeping turns while moving forward
The two species differed significantly at spinning turns but not at sweeping ones
Uneven flipper use affected how fast they could rotate
why_it_matters: Manoeuvrability matters for escaping predators and catching food, yet it had gone unmeasured in favour of long-distance endurance.

title: The genomic basis of independent marine transitions in turtles: convergent episodic adaptation and demographic shifts.
authors: Elisa Ramos, Leon Hilgers, Tomás Carrasco-Valenzuela, et al.
summary: Turtles moved from land into the sea more than once, independently. Comparing the genomes of green turtles, leatherbacks and a brackish-water terrapin shows all three remodelled the same kinds of genes, but not by the same genetic route.
key_points: Gene families for iron processing, organ development and sensory perception expanded in all three
The same patterns appear in other mammals and reptiles that returned to the sea
Despite hitting the same targets, no shared changes were found at the level of individual DNA letters
All three lineages went through deep population crashes in the distant past
why_it_matters: Evolution reaching the same solution by different molecular paths is a reminder that there is rarely only one way to adapt.

title: Interannual Fluctuations in Mean Straight Carapace Length (SCL) of Nesting Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtles Signal Demographic Shifts at Rancho Nuevo Sanctuary, Tamaulipas, Mexico.
authors: Kevin A Zavala-Félix, Fátima Yedith Camacho-Sánchez, Valeria Leal-Sepúlveda, et al.
summary: Kemp's ridley is the most endangered sea turtle, and the size of nesting females hints at how the population is doing. Measuring 191 females in Mexico over six seasons found their average size bounced around year to year without any real downward trend.
key_points: The population crashed from a 1947 peak to a 1985 low, recovered, then stalled after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill
Smallest average sizes came in 2020 and 2022, largest in 2018
Statistical testing found no significant decline across 2018 to 2023
The pattern looks like normal year-to-year variation rather than a worsening trend
why_it_matters: Distinguishing ordinary fluctuation from a genuine decline is the difference between a false alarm and a missed one.

title: Honu Count: how shell-etchings, participatory science, and a novel online survey are improving assessments of the Hawaiian Green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) population.
authors: Brittany L Clemans, Marylou K Staman, Irene K Kelly, et al.
summary: Hawaiian green turtles get a temporary identifier etched onto their shell so researchers can recognise individuals. Since 2017 the public has been reporting sightings of these marked turtles, and this paper describes how that volunteer data improved population estimates.
key_points: The main nesting site is an atoll about 1,000 km from the inhabited Hawaiian Islands
Official monitoring there has run continuously since 1973
Etchings are temporary, lasting 6 to 12 months, and sealed with non-toxic paint
Public sightings fill in where the turtles go between nesting seasons, which surveys at the nesting site cannot show
why_it_matters: Volunteer reporting covers ground that funded fieldwork cannot reach, and this shows how to make that data scientifically usable.

title: Osteological differences in the humerus of loggerhead and green turtles.
authors: Il-Kook Park, Suhwan Yoon, Hae Rim Lee, et al.
summary: Sea turtles swim almost entirely with their front flippers, so the upper arm bone carries the whole load. Measuring this bone in stranded loggerheads and green turtles from Korean waters found the two species differ in most of its dimensions.
key_points: Bones came from turtles found stranded or caught accidentally at the northern edge of their range
Arm bone length and width both scaled reliably with overall shell length
Twelve of fifteen measured segments differed significantly between the two species
That scaling means a turtle's size can be estimated from the bone alone
why_it_matters: Being able to identify species and body size from a single bone is useful when all that washes ashore is a partial carcass.

title: First Isolation of Yersinia enterocolitica From a Sea Turtle: A Case Report in Caretta caretta.
authors: Giorgia Schirò, Paola Galluzzo, Rosaria Disclafani, et al.
summary: A juvenile loggerhead turtle at an Italian rescue centre was found to be infected with Yersinia enterocolitica, a bacterium better known for causing food poisoning in people. It is the first time it has been isolated from any sea turtle.
key_points: The turtle arrived emaciated and dehydrated with severe anaemia, and died within days
An autopsy found a distended colon, internal adhesions and liver damage
Liver tissue showed inflammatory nodules with dead material at their centres
The exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, though the bacterium is a plausible contributor
why_it_matters: First records matter: a pathogen nobody is looking for in a species is a pathogen nobody will diagnose.

title: Which turtle should I study? Uneven distribution of research effort across Testudines species.
authors: Simon Ducatez, Jayna Lynn DeVore
summary: Two thirds of turtle species are threatened with extinction, but research attention is wildly uneven. This study counted published papers for every known species and found the green sea turtle alone has more studies than the least-studied half of all turtle species combined.
key_points: The green sea turtle accounts for 3,441 articles
All of the 50 percent least-studied species together total just 475 articles
The imbalance tracks with taxonomy, geography, ecology and evolutionary relationships
Results held up across two separate literature databases
why_it_matters: Conservation decisions rest on published evidence, so species nobody studies are species nobody can argue to protect.

title: Brevetoxicosis in loggerhead (Caretta caretta) and Kemp's ridley (Lepidochelys kempii) sea turtles: Plasma proteomics for Florida red tide biomarkers.
authors: Celina Ceballos, Kathleen S Rein, Catherine J Walsh
summary: Florida red tide produces potent neurotoxins that sicken sea turtles, but there is no proper diagnostic test. Researchers compared blood proteins in poisoned and healthy turtles to find markers that would confirm exposure.
key_points: Loggerhead and Kemp's ridley turtles were both studied
Turtles absorb the toxins by breathing in sea spray and by eating contaminated prey
Currently the only diagnostic is stranding during a bloom, which is circumstantial
Several blood proteins differed measurably between exposed and healthy animals
why_it_matters: Toxin exposure is often delayed by weeks as it works up the food chain, so a blood test would catch cases that timing alone would miss.

title: Disorientation patterns of loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta) hatchlings in Pinellas County, Florida, USA.
authors: Kerry L McNally, Carly Oakley, Megan Davila, et al.
summary: Hatchlings find the sea by following light cues, so artificial lighting sends them the wrong way. Six years of Florida nesting data show more than a third of nests produced hatchlings that crawled off in the wrong direction.
key_points: Of 1,048 nests that hatched between 2018 and 2023, 377 produced disoriented hatchlings
Nests higher up the beach fared significantly better than those in the middle
Problem areas clustered in particular spots, and the clustering shifted from year to year
Bright moonlight reduced disorientation, which supports artificial light as the cause
why_it_matters: Pinpointing which stretches of beach are worst lets councils target lighting rules where they will actually help.

title: Microplastics and sea turtle reproduction: A systematic review on nest contamination and developmental risks.
authors: Ragil Angga Prastiya, Suherni Susilowati, Imam Mustofa, et al.
summary: This review gathered every study it could find on microplastics in sea turtle nests worldwide. Plastic particles are not just on the sand surface, they reach down to the depth where eggs incubate and turn up inside the eggs and embryos themselves.
key_points: Contamination varied enormously by site, with over 12,000 particles per kilogram of dry sand on Redang Island, Malaysia
Polyethylene, polystyrene and PET dominated, mostly as fibres and foam
Particles were found in nest sediment, eggs, yolks and embryonic tissue
Studies spanned China, Malaysia, Mexico, Japan and the Mediterranean
why_it_matters: Plastic reaching inside the egg means the exposure starts before the animal has even hatched.

title: Protocol optimization for microplastic analysis in sea turtles: Including the first blood digestion method.
authors: Giulia de Andrade Lima Bertotti, Geraldo Jorge Barbosa de Moura, Gabriela Uchôa Souza de Medeiros, et al.
summary: Measuring microplastics inside an animal means dissolving the tissue without dissolving the plastic. This study worked out a reliable two-step recipe for sea turtle tissues and, for the first time, for blood.
key_points: The method covers blood, yolk sac, liver, kidney, muscle and reproductive tissue
It uses a potassium hydroxide digestion followed by hydrogen peroxide oxidation
Blood from nesting females was paired with yolk from their own eggs to test mother-to-egg transfer
Other tissues came from stranded turtles on the Brazilian northeast coast
why_it_matters: Without a shared method, microplastic counts from different labs cannot be compared, and a blood test opens up sampling live animals.

title: Plasma concentrations of terbinafine in Kemp's ridley sea turtles (Lepidochelys kempii) peak at 24 hours after a single oral dose.
authors: Sarah E Balik, Melissa J Joblon, Deana Edmunds, et al.
summary: Vets treating fungal infections in sea turtles had no dosing data for the antifungal drug terbinafine. Giving a single dose to 15 rehabilitating Kemp's ridley turtles showed the drug peaks in the blood a full 24 hours later.
key_points: The turtles were juveniles recovering from cold stunning in Massachusetts
The drug was hidden in food at 20 mg per kg of body weight
Blood levels peaked at 24 hours and the drug took about the same time to halve
Blood samples were collected across five days after the dose
why_it_matters: Dosing a reptile on numbers borrowed from mammals is guesswork, and fungal infections are a common killer in turtle rehabilitation.

title: Physics-informed multi-task learning framework for modelling microplastic impacts on sea turtle nest temperature and sex determination.
authors: Danang A Pratama, Aina Arifah Khalid, Ummu Atiqah Mohd Roslan, et al.
summary: Plastic in nesting sand may change how hot a nest gets, which matters because temperature decides hatchling sex. This team built a prediction model that respects the known physics of sex determination and used it on green turtle nests in Malaysia.
key_points: Three nesting sites in Terengganu were studied, with plastic profiled by colour, shape, size and depth
The model predicts nest temperature and sex ratio together rather than separately
It beat standard machine-learning approaches, with the lowest temperature error and perfect sex-ratio classification
Building the physics in kept its predictions consistent with how sex determination actually works
why_it_matters: A model that cannot violate the underlying biology is more trustworthy than one that merely fits the data well.

title: Pathology of green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas): Mortalities in Gladstone Harbour, Queensland, Australia, 2017-2020.
authors: Christabel Hannon, Helen Owen, Helle Bielefeldt-Ohmann
summary: Gladstone Harbour in Queensland is both an important green turtle feeding ground and the site of a huge coal port. Autopsies on 22 stranded turtles over four years catalogued what is actually killing them there.
key_points: The harbour hosts juvenile, near-adult and adult green turtles year round
A century of port expansion has degraded seagrass beds and mangroves and increased shipping and pollution
Turtles examined were either found dead or euthanised because they could not be saved
The work was part of a monitoring programme tied specifically to the port
why_it_matters: When industry and a feeding ground occupy the same water, cause-of-death records are the evidence base for arguing about impact.

title: Comparative Analysis of Nasal and Cloacal Bacterial Communities in Three Sea Turtle Species under Rescue Center Conditions.
authors: Xinyi Yang, Jiao Tang, Zhuoxin Lai, et al.
summary: Rescued turtles carry bacterial communities in their noses and cloacas that nobody had properly surveyed. Sequencing three species at a Chinese rescue station found the nose community is remarkably sensitive to how the turtle is housed.
key_points: Green, hawksbill and olive ridley turtles were all sampled
Housing conditions explained more than half the variation in green turtle nasal bacteria
Outdoor turtles developed a distinctly different nasal community from indoor ones
Turtles with facial injuries carried their own recognisable bacterial signatures
why_it_matters: If a husbandry choice as simple as indoors versus outdoors reshapes the microbiome, rehabilitation protocols are shaping turtle health in ways nobody was tracking.

title: Predation on sea turtles at sea: A multi-source synthesis and research perspectives.
authors: Paolo Casale, Alessandro Servolini, Enrique González-Bernardo, et al.
summary: Predation on turtle eggs and hatchlings on beaches is well documented, but what eats turtles at sea is far harder to observe. This synthesis pooled field records, literature, predator stomach contents and even online photos and videos to build a global picture.
key_points: Records covered all seven sea turtle species and 51 different predator species
Of 156,726 turtle records examined, 3.3 percent showed shark-bite injuries
Predators ranged across fish, crocodilians and mammals, but a handful of shark species dominate
Predation rates varied significantly by turtle species, body size, region and over time
why_it_matters: Using unconventional sources like social media images is how you measure something that is nearly impossible to witness directly.

title: Hidden Markov models reveal ontogenetic plasticity in green and loggerhead sea turtles.
authors: Ryan C Welsh, Katherine L Mansfield
summary: Turtle conservation usually sorts animals into life stages by size or location. Applying a behaviour-first statistical model to 47 years of Florida capture records found three behavioural types that do not line up neatly with size at all.
key_points: Nearly 20,000 capture events for green and loggerhead turtles were analysed
The model identified nomadic, resident and transient behaviour patterns
Nomads were smaller and rarely recaptured; residents stayed put; transients were larger and seasonal
Size ranges for each behaviour overlapped, undermining rigid size-based stage labels
why_it_matters: Managing turtles by size category misses animals that behave nothing like their size suggests they should.

title: Juveniles and where to find them: a basin-scale habitat model for the lost years of loggerhead sea turtles in the North Atlantic.
authors: M Bartolini, E L Hazen, H Parra, et al.
summary: Young loggerheads spend years crossing the open Atlantic in what researchers call the lost years, and almost nobody knows where they go. Pooling satellite tracks from 124 juveniles produced the first habitat map for the entire ocean basin.
key_points: Turtles were tagged around the Azores, Canary Islands, Madeira and the western Atlantic
Seventeen environmental variables were tested to find what predicts where juveniles go
The final model was highly accurate and was used to map suitable habitat from 1998 to 2022
Stranding records from France, the UK and Ireland were used as an independent check
why_it_matters: Juveniles crossing the Atlantic run a gauntlet of fishing fleets, and you cannot reduce that overlap without knowing their route.

title: Anatomic Interactive Atlas of the Loggerhead Sea Turtle (Caretta caretta) Coelomic Cavity.
authors: Alberto Arencibia, Aday Melián, Jorge Orós
summary: Vets treating sea turtles need to know what healthy insides look like before they can spot what is wrong. This team built a free interactive atlas of the loggerhead body cavity from dissections, CT scans and MRI.
key_points: It combines six skeleton images, sixteen dissection photographs, fourteen MRI scans and CT in several formats
Every anatomical structure is colour-coded and labelled by hand
The images are delivered through an interactive interface rather than as a flat reference
The whole thing is open access
why_it_matters: Turtle medicine is held back by a shortage of basic reference material, and a free atlas removes that barrier for any clinic.

title: Artificial night lighting in the Mediterranean: Management priorities and constraints for sea turtle conservation.
authors: Charalampos Dimitriadis, Nikolaos Simantiris, Fulvio Maffucci, et al.
summary: Artificial light at night disrupts turtle nesting, but its scale around the Mediterranean was unmeasured. Surveying 27 experts across 16 countries produced a ranked list of what to do about it and what is stopping anyone doing it.
key_points: Experts agreed hatchlings are the most vulnerable stage, especially while finding the sea
Light causes disorientation, raises predation risk and reduces how many hatchlings survive
Standardised monitoring of light pollution is essentially absent, mainly for lack of funding
Top fixes: shielded downward-facing long-wavelength lighting, shaded corridors and nature-based solutions
why_it_matters: Pooling expert judgement produces an actionable priority list far faster than waiting for monitoring programmes that nobody is funding.

title: Metal Concentrations (Mg, Fe, Zn, Cu, Cd, Pb) in the Plasma and Cell Concentrates of Chelonia mydas and Lepidochelys olivacea from Costa Rica.
authors: Cecilia Rudelli, Gloria Isani, Micaela Fabbri, et al.
summary: Blood is an attractive way to monitor pollution in living turtles, but there is little baseline data. This study measured six metals in green turtles and olive ridleys from both Costa Rican coasts and compared the results to studies over the following two decades.
key_points: Samples came from 2003 to 2004 on the Caribbean and Pacific coasts
Metals distributed unevenly: magnesium and copper concentrated in plasma, iron and zinc in blood cells
Green turtles carried more copper, iron and zinc; olive ridleys markedly more cadmium
Separating plasma from cells matters, since testing whole blood would blur these differences
why_it_matters: Historical baselines are what let anyone say whether pollution today is better or worse than before.

title: Warming and Change in Ocean Productivity Alter Phenology of an Expanding Loggerhead Population in Cabo Verde.
authors: Fitra Arya Dwi Nugraha, Kirsten Fairweather, Artur Lopes, et al.
summary: Seventeen years of monitoring one of the world's largest loggerhead populations in Cabo Verde shows warming seas are shifting when the turtles nest and reducing how much they produce.
key_points: Warmer sea temperatures pulled the start, peak and end of the nesting season earlier
Females arrive in distinct waves, implying more turtles each laying fewer clutches than assumed
Gaps between nesting attempts shortened in warm spells, especially in larger females
Falling ocean productivity at the feeding grounds reduced clutch size, clutch frequency and body size
why_it_matters: Earlier nesting looks like successful adaptation until you notice the food supply is shrinking at the same time.

title: Divergence and conservation of satellite DNA in the loggerhead sea turtle (Caretta caretta): a comparative cytogenomic analysis.
authors: Katerina V Tishakova, Anastasia A Proskuryakova, Dmitry Yu Prokopov, et al.
summary: Large stretches of any genome are repetitive sequence that gets ignored. This study catalogued the repeat landscape of the loggerhead turtle genome and mapped it onto individual chromosomes.
key_points: At least 18 distinct families of repetitive sequence were identified
Most cluster near the centres of chromosomes
Some chromosomes carry a single signature repeat; others hold complex mixtures
Comparison with existing assemblies turned up inconsistencies worth resolving
why_it_matters: Repetitive regions are where genome assemblies most often go wrong, so mapping them physically is a check on the digital version.

title: Reorganisation of the turtle blood fluke genera Hapalotrema and Learedius (Trematoda: Hapalotrematidae), with the proposal of two new genera, a new species, and comments on population structure.
authors: Richard D Corner, Thomas H Cribb, Scott C Cutmore
summary: Blood flukes are the most commonly reported parasites of marine turtles, but their classification was a mess, with species of one genus scattered among another on the family tree. This study reorganised the group, proposing two new genera and one new species.
key_points: The parasites infect many organs but turn up most often in the heart and major vessels
Morphology and DNA from several genes were combined to untangle the relationships
It includes the first record of an adult turtle blood fluke from an olive ridley
Genetic variation differed sharply between species, with several distinct populations along the Queensland coast
why_it_matters: Parasites you cannot name consistently are parasites you cannot track, and these are among the most common that turtles carry.

title: Perivitelline Membrane-Bound Sperm as a Source of Paternal Genomic DNA to Inform Breeding Male Marine Turtle Genetics and Demographics.
authors: Brian M Shamblin, Cheryl L Sanchez, Sean M Perry, et al.
summary: Nobody knows much about male sea turtles because they never come ashore. This study worked out how to genotype the father from sperm trapped in the membrane around a single egg's yolk.
key_points: Loggerhead and green turtle eggs from Melbourne Beach, Florida were tested
Results were checked against the genotypes of more than 1,700 actual hatchlings
The method correctly identified all but two of 67 fathers
It needs only one egg per nest rather than sampling many hatchlings
why_it_matters: Warming sand is producing ever more females, and you cannot monitor that risk without a way to count the breeding males.

title: Behavioral responses of captive-bred post-hatchling and juvenile sea turtles to different colors of single-use plastic film.
authors: Yelim Moon, Hee-Jin Noh, Gi Myung Han, et al.
summary: Turtles eat plastic, but which plastic and why is unclear. Offering captive-bred hawksbills different coloured films showed juveniles have clear preferences while very young hatchlings bite at anything.
key_points: Eight four-year-old juveniles and twenty-seven ten-week-old post-hatchlings were tested
Juveniles went for transparent, white, black and yellow items but ignored blue bottle labels
They preferred soft plastic bags over stiffer packaging
Post-hatchlings showed no preference, probably because they have not learned to recognise prey yet
why_it_matters: If turtles are selectively eating light-coloured soft plastic because it resembles jellyfish, that points at which products matter most to eliminate.

title: Confirmation of Chelonid Alphaherpesvirus 5 (Scutavirus Chelonidalpha5) Associated with Fibropapillomatosis in Green and Kemp's Ridley Sea Turtles from Mississippi, USA.
authors: Sarah A Rubelowsky, Justin M Stilwell, Caroline Betbeze, et al.
summary: Fibropapillomatosis, the tumour disease of sea turtles, was confirmed along with its associated herpesvirus in four turtles stranded on the Mississippi coast. It extends the documented range of the disease in the Gulf of Mexico.
key_points: Three green turtles and one Kemp's ridley were involved
Both the tumours and the virus were confirmed by laboratory testing rather than appearance alone
All four animals stranded on the Mississippi coast
The finding fills in a gap in the known distribution of the disease
why_it_matters: Range extensions for a wildlife disease are early warnings, and they only get recorded if someone tests the strandings.

title: Underwater hearing sensitivity of the Kemp's ridley sea turtle (Lepidochelys kempii).
authors: Charles A Muirhead, Wendy E D Piniak, Douglas P Nowacek, et al.
summary: Shipping and offshore energy fill the waters where Kemp's ridley turtles live, but nobody knew what they can hear. Testing 13 juveniles by measuring brain responses to underwater tones mapped their hearing range for the first time.
key_points: They responded to sounds between 50 and 800 Hz, all low frequencies
Hearing was sharpest between 200 and 300 Hz and fell away above 400 Hz
Nothing registered at 1200 Hz or above, even at high volume
Their most sensitive threshold averaged 100 decibels at 300 Hz
why_it_matters: You cannot write noise limits to protect an animal until you know which frequencies it can actually hear.

title: They're Out There, You Know: Sea Turtle Sightings and Strandings in Canadian Pacific Waters.
authors: Lisa Spaven, Amy Migneault, Karina Dracott, et al.
summary: British Columbia is far colder than sea turtles normally tolerate, yet they turn up there. This paper compiles every known record from Canadian Pacific waters between 1931 and 2024, including 77 never published before.
key_points: The dataset holds 247 records across four species
Leatherbacks were most common and were usually seen alive and swimming
Nearly half of hard-shelled turtles were found dead or cold-stunned
Leatherbacks can regulate their body temperature; hard-shelled species cannot, which explains the split
why_it_matters: Records at the cold edge of a species range are exactly the records that will show whether warming seas are shifting that edge.

title: Biomarkers of foraging and reproduction in captive adult female hawksbill sea turtles (Eretmochelys imbricata).
authors: Joslyn Blessing Kent, Kari Renee Dawson, Shingo Fukada, et al.
summary: Wild hawksbill turtles can usually only be sampled while nesting, so nobody knows what their normal non-breeding physiology looks like. Following five captive females for a full year in a Japanese aquarium filled that gap.
key_points: Blood was tested for fat-burning markers and the hormone testosterone across all seasons
Both fat-burning markers rose significantly while the reproductive organs were developing
Having year-round data shows which readings are normal and which are specific to nesting
Hawksbills are listed as critically endangered, making baseline physiology valuable
why_it_matters: Without off-season measurements, every nesting-season reading is uninterpretable because there is nothing to compare it against.

title: Influence of Nest Microbiota on Hatching Success of Caretta Caretta on Lampedusa Island.
authors: Fanny Claire Capri, Elena Prazzi, Giulia Casamento, et al.
summary: Why do some turtle nests hatch almost completely while others fail entirely? Comparing bacteria in four loggerhead nests on Lampedusa found the one successful nest had a clearly different bacterial community from the three that failed.
key_points: Hatching success ranged from 85.2 percent in the successful nest down to 0 percent
Sand, eggshells and inner egg membranes were all sampled and sequenced
The successful nest separated statistically from the failures on community composition
The balance between two major bacterial groups was distinctly different in the successful nest
why_it_matters: If nest bacteria help decide whether eggs hatch, that is a factor hatchery managers could potentially influence.

title: Occurrence of Citrobacter spp.-Associated and Non-Associated Lesions in a Stranded Loggerhead Sea Turtle (Caretta caretta) from Italy.
authors: Filippo Fratini, Rossana Schena, Sinem Arslan, et al.
summary: Turtle skin naturally carries many bacteria, some of which cause ulcerating disease. Swabbing a loggerhead at an Italian aquarium recovered fifteen strains of one such bacterium and tested how drug-resistant they were.
key_points: Nine swabs were taken from skin lesions, shell, mouth and cloaca
Strains were tested against twelve antimicrobials spanning eight drug classes
They were screened for genes conferring resistance to major antibiotic families
Their ability to form biofilm, which protects bacteria from treatment, was also measured
why_it_matters: Turtles in human care can act as reservoirs for drug-resistant bacteria, which makes this a staff safety question as well as an animal health one.

title: Between the Atolls: Sea Turtle Nesting in the Maldives from 2018 to 2024.
authors: Isha Afeef, Jane R Lloyd, Ibrahim Inan, et al.
summary: The Maldives had no comprehensive nesting record despite turtles being central to its marine ecosystem. Combining targeted monitoring with reports from citizen scientists and biologists produced the first multi-year dataset, covering 2018 to 2024.
key_points: Nests were recorded on nearly every atoll, overwhelmingly green turtles at 1,086 nests
Hawksbill, olive ridley and unidentified nests made up the small remainder
Nesting happens year-round but peaks June to September during the southwest monsoon
Median hatching success was 90.9 percent over a median 59-day incubation
why_it_matters: Flooding and illegal egg collection emerged as the main threats, which is actionable in a way that an unquantified problem is not.

title: Genomic Differentiation and Diversity in Persian Gulf Hawksbill Turtles (Eretmochelys imbricata) Revealed by the First Whole-Genome Sequencing Study.
authors: Mohammadali Farahvashi, Mohammadreza Mohammadabadi, Majid Askari-Hesni, et al.
summary: This is the first whole-genome study of hawksbill turtles in the Persian Gulf. Sequencing 17 turtles from four Iranian nesting islands found genetically distinct populations even between islands close together.
key_points: Four separate populations emerged from the genetic data
One island showed long-term isolation while another showed mixing and higher diversity
Genetic patterns point to historical population crashes rather than recent inbreeding
Females returning to their own birth beach appears to drive the separation
why_it_matters: Nearby islands holding genetically distinct turtles means each one needs its own conservation plan rather than a single regional approach.

title: Major Histocompatibility Complex Immunogenetic Diversity Differs Substantially Across Sea Turtle Species and Genomic Regions.
authors: Katherine R Martin, Jamie L Adkins, Vipheaviny Chea, et al.
summary: Immune system genes are usually extremely varied, because variety helps a population survive new diseases. Sequencing these genes in over 300 turtles across four species found the amount of variation differs dramatically between species.
key_points: Loggerhead, green, leatherback and Kemp's ridley turtles were compared
162 and 308 functionally distinct versions were found in the two gene classes examined
Many versions are shared between species, meaning they predate the species splitting apart
Evidence of ongoing natural selection suggests the variety is being actively maintained
why_it_matters: A species with little immune variation is a species with little room to respond to a new disease, which matters given the tumour outbreaks turtles already face.

title: Molecular signatures and cellular responses underlying hypoxic adaptation in sea turtles.
authors: B Gabriela Arango, Giovanna Selleghin-Veiga, Diana Daniela Moreno-Santillán, et al.
summary: Sea turtles hold their breath for remarkably long dives, and this preprint looked for the genetic basis. Comparing low-oxygen response genes across reptiles found one of them is under active evolutionary pressure specifically in turtles.
key_points: Three of the four genes examined are highly conserved across all reptiles
The fourth shows signs of positive selection in turtles and tortoises specifically
Several regulatory sequences appear unique to the turtle lineage
Loggerhead cells responded to low oxygen quite differently from lizard cells
why_it_matters: Understanding how turtles tolerate oxygen deprivation is relevant to why some survive being caught in nets and others do not.

title: Somatic Growth Rates of Juvenile Green Sea Turtles (Chelonia mydas) in the Fijian Archipelago.
authors: Garrett E Lemons, Calandra N Turner Tomaszewicz, Shritika Prakash, et al.
summary: How fast turtles grow tells you how long they take to reach breeding age, which drives every population projection. Measuring 215 green turtles across three Fijian feeding areas over seven years produced the first growth rates for the region.
key_points: Turtles grew an average of 1.6 cm of shell length per year
Growth rates varied between the three sites, from 1.1 to 1.8 cm per year
Growth slowed as turtles got larger
The Fijian figures line up with those from elsewhere in the Pacific
why_it_matters: Site-to-site differences in growth suggest some feeding grounds are simply better habitat than others, which is a conservation priority signal.

title: Hazardous seascapes for marine turtles in the Mediterranean sea.
authors: G Quattrocchi, G Cilluffo, G Buffa, et al.
summary: Which parts of the Mediterranean are most dangerous for turtles? By working backwards from where carcasses washed ashore, researchers reconstructed where the deaths actually happened and compared that against fishing traffic and floating litter.
key_points: Five years of stranding data around Sicily and Sardinia fed a drift model
Reconstructed death locations overlapped strongly with dense fishing vessel routes
The link to floating debris was much weaker and more diffuse
The analysis allowed hazard levels to vary from place to place rather than assuming one pattern
why_it_matters: Fishing traffic showing a far tighter link to mortality than litter tells managers which threat to spend their limited budget on.

title: Green Sea Turtle Recruitment in the Eastern North Pacific: Patterns Identified Using Geochemical Signatures in Bones.
authors: Calandra N Turner Tomaszewicz, Erin LaCasella, Garrett E Lemons, et al.
summary: Green turtles have become increasingly common off urban Southern California over three decades. Reading the chemical layers in turtle arm bones, like tree rings, reconstructed where individual turtles had been feeding through their lives.
key_points: Ocean chemistry varies predictably by region and gets locked into bone as it grows
Bone growth layers were paired with age and size estimates from the same bones
This reconstructed each turtle's movement and diet history retrospectively
The method works on dead turtles, requiring no tracking equipment
why_it_matters: Extracting a lifetime movement history from a bone means dead strandings become data rather than just losses.

title: Blood analytes relevant to nutritional status and energy metabolism in three sea turtle species across nesting season.
authors: Kristina L Kaleel, Justin R Perrault, Sarah E Hirsch, et al.
summary: Nesting is physiologically brutal, and vets need to know what normal blood chemistry looks like during it. This study established reference ranges across three to four nesting seasons for three species.
key_points: Leatherback, loggerhead and green turtles were all sampled
Measures covered blood cell volume, fat-burning markers, protein, glucose and lactate
Leatherbacks showed significant declines in four of the measures as the season progressed
The study also tested how much delayed sample processing distorts results
why_it_matters: Without reference ranges a vet cannot tell a sick nesting turtle from a normally exhausted one.

title: Rediscovering nesting activities of Lepidochelys olivacea along the Dakshina Kannada Coast Karnataka West Coast of India.
authors: Thejaswini Shettigar, Shivakumar Haragi, Anthony Mariyappa
summary: Olive ridley turtles nested on India's Dakshina Kannada coast for the first time in 18 years. Twenty-one nests appeared across six beaches in a single season, including on busy commercial stretches.
key_points: One beach near Mangalore accounted for 62 percent of all nests
Nesting happened across all moon phases, contradicting the expected full-moon preference
Clutches held 71 to 135 eggs and incubated for about 49 days
Nests closer to river mouths had better hatching success
why_it_matters: A nesting population returning after 18 years is a conservation win, and documenting it is what secures protection for those beaches.

title: Prevalence, etiology, and transmission of fibropapillomatosis in Olive Ridley turtles at a mass-nesting colony in the Mexican Pacific.
authors: Elizabeth Labastida-Estrada, Karina Marisol Lugo-Trejo, Valentina Islas-Villanueva, et al.
summary: At one of the world's great mass-nesting beaches in Oaxaca, Mexico, researchers measured how common the turtle tumour disease is and tested whether parasitic leeches spread it.
key_points: Disease prevalence among nesting olive ridley females was low, about 1.05 percent
Viral DNA was sought in both tumours and healthy tissue from affected and unaffected turtles
Marine leeches taken from both groups were screened as possible carriers
Genetic variants of the virus were identified from both turtles and leeches
why_it_matters: If leeches transmit the virus, that opens a route to interrupting the disease that treating turtles alone never could.

title: Performance Comparison of Argos and Iridium Tracking Technologies for Sea Turtle Movement Ecology Studies.
authors: Paolo Casale, Christine Figgener, Michael Arendt, et al.
summary: Satellite tags for turtles come in several technologies, and researchers need to know which actually performs best. Comparing 116,074 positions from 48 turtles found clear differences between the three tag types.
key_points: Five species across multiple ocean basins were included
Tags were judged on how many days returned data, gap length, and positions per day
The three types compared were older Doppler-based, GPS-enhanced, and newer GPS tags on a different satellite network
Species and tag settings also affected performance, not just the technology
why_it_matters: Tags are expensive and go on endangered animals, so choosing the wrong one wastes both money and a rare research opportunity.

title: Predation by Native Mediterranean Species on the Invasive Blue Crab: Experimental Evidence from the Common Octopus and the Loggerhead Sea Turtle.
authors: Silvia Falco, Miguel Rodilla, José Luis Crespo-Picazo, et al.
summary: Invasive blue crabs are overrunning Mediterranean coasts, so researchers asked whether native predators could help control them. Aquarium trials pitted octopuses and loggerhead turtles against crabs of various sizes.
key_points: Turtles ate crabs whole, shell included, consuming up to 815 g per day
Octopuses ate only the soft tissue, about 54 percent of each crab, up to 454 g per day
Neither predator showed a statistically clear preference for particular crab sizes
Smaller octopuses handled small crabs faster than large ones
why_it_matters: Turtles eating invasive crabs whole is a rare case where a threatened species might help solve another ecological problem.

title: Dynamics of fibropapillomatosis in green turtles Chelonia mydas from Babitonga Bay, southern Brazil.
authors: Tiago Fernando Alves, Marta Jussara Cremer
summary: Babitonga Bay in southern Brazil turns out to be a hotspot for the turtle tumour disease. Monitoring 171 juvenile green turtles over five years found more than half were affected, among the highest rates recorded in the country.
key_points: Prevalence reached 53.2 percent
Tumours clustered around the flippers and armpit area and were mostly small
Disease severity showed no clear link to the turtle's body condition
Recaptured turtles showed tumours both growing and shrinking over time
why_it_matters: Tumours regressing on their own in some animals suggests environmental conditions influence the disease, not just the virus.

title: Anthropogenic stones on a remote oceanic island: formation, transport, and burial in a sea turtle nesting beach.
authors: Fernanda Avelar Santos, Matheus Brito da Silva, Giovana Rebelo Diorio, et al.
summary: Plastic can melt and fuse with rock to form something geologists now call plastistone. Five years of monitoring a remote green turtle nesting beach in the South Atlantic tracked how these masses break apart and spread.
key_points: An original plastistone deposit shrank 45 percent between 2019 and 2024 as it eroded
The fragments spread to six different beaches on the island
Fragments accumulate in the strandline at roughly 24 larger and 22 smaller pieces per square metre
They are also found inside turtle nesting pits, buried to about 10 cm deep
why_it_matters: Plastic turning into a rock-like material that then erodes into nests is a pollution pathway nobody was tracking a decade ago.

title: An application of finite element analysis predicts unique temperatures and fates for flatback sea turtle embryos.
authors: Malindi Gammon, Sabrina Fossette, Ali Karrech, et al.
summary: Nest temperature is usually measured with a single logger, which ignores the fact that embryos themselves generate heat. Applying engineering simulation software to flatback turtle nests predicted a different temperature for every individual egg.
key_points: Five nests were modelled using clutch size, depth, sand density and moisture
Each egg was given its own hourly heat output based on its metabolic rate
Predictions were checked against real measured nest temperatures
Eggs in different positions experience meaningfully different conditions
why_it_matters: If eggs in the same nest incubate at different temperatures, they may be destined for different sexes and different survival odds.

title: Mycobacterium ulcerans ecovar infection in wild Kemp's ridley Lepidochelys kempii and loggerhead Caretta caretta sea turtles.
authors: Brian A Stacy, Robert J Ossiboff, Allyson L McNaughton, et al.
summary: Six wild turtles were found infected with a relative of the bacterium that causes Buruli ulcer in humans, and in most cases it had reached the brain. Four of the six were found near one another with no obvious reason to be vulnerable.
key_points: Five Kemp's ridley turtles and one loggerhead were affected
Most stranded showing neurological problems caused by severe brain and spinal inflammation
The immune response failed to wall the bacteria off in the nervous system the way it normally would
Genetic testing matched the strains across multiple sites in the genome
why_it_matters: Healthy turtles clustered together falling ill points at an environmental source rather than isolated bad luck, which has population-level implications.

title: Imaging-guided clinical approach to fishing line ingestion in a juvenile green sea turtle Chelonia mydas from southern Brazil.
authors: Yohany Arnold Alfonso Pérez, Gustavo Martinez-Souza, Thayana Gião, et al.
summary: A juvenile green turtle was found during fishing monitoring in Brazil with fishing line hanging from its mouth. Imaging showed exactly how far the line ran before anyone pulled on it, which is what made safe removal possible.
key_points: X-ray and ultrasound traced the line through mouth, throat and stomach
Crucially, no hooks were attached, so the line could be withdrawn by hand
Blood tests showed anaemia, elevated white cells and raised urea from gut injury
The turtle's body was already mounting a systemic response to the trauma
why_it_matters: Pulling on a swallowed line without imaging first can tear the gut if a hook is anchored, so this is a procedural lesson as much as a case report.

title: Modelling the pipping to emergence interval and its influence on the thermosensitive period for sex determination in the green sea turtle Cheloniamydas.
authors: Kirsty Scott, Jesse E M Cochran, Royale S Hardenstine, et al.
summary: Hatchlings break out of the egg days before they dig their way to the surface, and that gap muddles the temperature calculations used to predict sex ratios. This study measured the hidden interval using motion sensors buried in nests.
key_points: Field studies time incubation to emergence; lab studies time it to hatching, which are not the same thing
Accelerometers detected the movement of hatching beneath the sand
The gap can span several days, shifting estimates of when sex is actually determined
Work focused on a green turtle population already under thermal stress in the northwest Indian Ocean
why_it_matters: If the window when sex gets decided is being mis-timed, then climate predictions built on it are off too.

title: Disruption of the sea turtle magnetic map sense by a magnetic pulse.
authors: Alayna G Mackiewicz, Abigail M Glazener, Kayla M Goforth, et al.
summary: Sea turtles navigate using Earth's magnetic field, but how they sense it was unknown. Hitting loggerheads with a brief strong magnetic pulse disrupted their ability to tell where they were, pointing to tiny magnetic crystals as the sensor.
key_points: The pulse is strong enough to flip the magnetic polarity of the mineral magnetite
A conditioning test was used that needs the turtles' magnetic map but not their compass
That separation matters, because previous experiments could not tell the two senses apart
The disruption implicates magnetite-based receptors in the map sense specifically
why_it_matters: Pinning down the physical mechanism behind turtle navigation is the step that makes it possible to ask how human magnetic interference might affect them.

title: A quantitative risk assessment framework for mortality due to macroplastic ingestion in seabirds, marine mammals, and sea turtles.
authors: Erin L Murphy, Britta R Baechler, Lauren Roman, et al.
summary: Plastic has been found in nearly 1,300 marine species, but how much is actually lethal? Analysing over 10,000 autopsies produced the first quantitative estimate of fatal dose for seabirds, marine mammals and sea turtles.
key_points: 47 percent of sea turtles examined had eaten plastic, the highest of the three groups
Seabirds were at 35 percent and marine mammals 12 percent
Risk was modelled against both the number of pieces and their volume relative to body length
Hard plastic, soft plastic, rubber and fishing debris were assessed separately
why_it_matters: Turning plastic ingestion from an alarming statistic into a dose-response relationship is what lets regulators argue about specific thresholds.

title: Cretaceous sea turtle soft tissues clarify ancestry of scale loss in chelonioids.
authors: Benjamin P Kear, Roy Nohra, Johan Lindgren, et al.
summary: The leatherback turtle has smooth skin while other sea turtles have scales, and nobody knew which came first. A 97-million-year-old fossil from Lebanon, the oldest sea turtle soft tissue known, settles it.
key_points: The fossil combines scale-free flipper skin with a scuted shell
Scale-free skin turns out to be an ancient sea turtle trait, not a leatherback innovation
Modern hard-shelled turtles therefore re-evolved their scaly flippers
The same smooth-skin adaptation appeared independently in ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and marine crocodiles
why_it_matters: Soft tissue almost never fossilises, so a 97-million-year-old skin impression can resolve a question bones cannot.

title: Anatomopathological Characterization of the Main Ocular Lesions in Green Turtles (Chelonia mydas) Along the Northern Coast of Bahia, Brazil.
authors: Danielle Nascimento Silva, José Luís Catão-Dias, Wendell Marcelo de Souza Perinotto, et al.
summary: Thirty-nine stranded green turtles in Bahia, Brazil had their eyes and tear glands examined in detail. Nearly seven in ten samples showed disease, most often tumours and parasites.
key_points: Of 158 samples from eyelids, eyes and salt glands, 69.6 percent were diseased
Fibropapillomatosis was the most common finding at 58.9 percent, followed by blood flukes at 46.8 percent
Most problems affected both eyes rather than one
Other findings included corneal ulcers, perforations, scarring and stones in the salt glands
why_it_matters: A blind turtle cannot feed or avoid boats, so eye disease at this rate is a survival issue and not a cosmetic one.

title: Power analyses to inform clutch sampling design to determine the breeding sex ratio in populations with multiple paternity.
authors: Vic Quennessen, Mariana M B P Fuentes, Lisa Komoroske, et al.
summary: Working out how many males are breeding in a population means genotyping eggs, but how many eggs do you actually need? This study calculated the sampling effort required to be confident you have found every father.
key_points: The answer depends on whether fathers contribute equally or one dominates each clutch
Effort can be spent on more eggs per nest or more nests per season, a real trade-off
Under-sampling means missing fathers and overestimating how female-biased a population is
Guidance covers both single clutches and whole nesting seasons
why_it_matters: Field budgets are finite, and this tells researchers the minimum sampling that still produces a defensible answer.

title: Metagenomic insights reveal the differences in the community composition and functional characteristics of the sea turtle microbiomes based on host species and tissue region.
authors: Lingzhi Dong, Yu Du, Feifei Qiu, et al.
summary: This study built the first comprehensive gene catalogue for sea turtle microbes, sequencing mouth, nose and cloaca samples from three species. Which body site a sample came from mattered more than which species it came from.
key_points: Sixty-three samples produced about 706 gigabytes of sequence data
The resulting catalogue holds over 10.7 million unique microbial genes
Two bacterial groups dominated across all sites and species
Green turtles showed the most variation between body regions
why_it_matters: A reference catalogue is infrastructure: every future study of turtle microbes can now compare against it instead of starting over.

title: Recombinant expression and functional characterization of defensin-like peptide TEWP and its analogs in Pichia pastoris.
authors: Saime Gülsüm Batman, Zülal Kesmen
summary: Turtle egg whites contain a natural antimicrobial protein. Researchers produced it in yeast along with three redesigned versions, then tested all four against nineteen microbes.
key_points: The original protein comes from loggerhead sea turtle eggs
Variants were made by swapping amino acids, reversing the sequence, and attaching a cell-entry tag
All versions worked best against Listeria monocytogenes, a serious food-borne bacterium
Simply increasing the protein's electrical charge did not improve its potency
why_it_matters: Natural antimicrobials are a hunting ground for new antibiotics, and producing them in yeast means no turtles are needed to make them.

title: First Survey on Sea Turtles' Interactions in Mussel Farms in Italy.
authors: Ludovica Di Renzo, Giulia Mariani, Marco Matiddi, et al.
summary: Loggerhead turtles have learned that mussel farms are an easy meal, which is a problem for the farmers. Surveying Italian mussel growers alongside autopsies of stranded turtles confirmed the turtles really are eating farmed mussels.
key_points: Sightings peaked in summer in the northern Adriatic and in autumn further south, tracking water temperature
Mediterranean mussel was the most commonly found mollusc in turtle stomachs
Its presence in turtle guts rose noticeably between 2018 and 2021
National data on the scale of the conflict had never been gathered before
why_it_matters: Conservation needs the fishing industry on side, so a conflict like this is better measured than ignored.

title: Long-Term Incubation Duration Decline Indicates Climate-Change Driven Feminization of Three Sea Turtle Species in Florida, USA.
authors: Simona A Ceriani, Paolo Casale
summary: Turtle sex is set by nest temperature, and warmer nests mean more females. Using incubation time as a thermometer across more than 110,000 Florida nests gives the first large-scale evidence that three species really are becoming more female.
key_points: Data spanned 2001 to 2022 and covered loggerhead, green and leatherback turtles
Incubation times declined significantly, which indicates rising nest temperatures
Using incubation duration sidesteps the uncertainty in model-based sex ratio estimates
Embryo death rates varied between regions as well
why_it_matters: Feminisation had been predicted by models for years; this is the population-scale measurement showing it is actually happening.

title: Total mercury levels in Loggerhead and Green sea turtle hatched eggshells from nests along the southeastern Mediterranean coast.
authors: Jacob Silverman, Orin Levin, Yaniv Levy, et al.
summary: Mercury accumulates in turtles over their lives and gets passed into their eggs. Measuring it in hatched eggshells from Israeli beaches is a way to gauge the mothers' contamination without disturbing anything.
key_points: 180 loggerhead and 40 green turtle eggshells were analysed across two nesting seasons
Loggerhead eggshells held about six times more mercury than green turtle eggshells
